Estimate a ratio of two population totals

Source: R/estimate.R
ht_ratio.Rd

ht_ratio() estimates R = Y / X, the ratio of the population totals of y and x, by sum(y / pi) / sum(x / pi): audited value per unit of book value, spend per visit, or yield per hectare. A Hajek mean is the ratio with x equal to 1 in every row. ht_total() with ratio multiplies the ratio by the frame's total of x to estimate the total of y.

Usage

ht_ratio(
  sample,
  y,
  x,
  by = NULL,
  variance = c("auto", "analytic", "jackknife", "none"),
  level = 0.95,
  df = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater")
)

Arguments

sample

A data frame returned by draw() with weights = TRUE. See "Which columns are read".

y, x

The numerator and the denominator: each a column name of sample, or a numeric vector as long as sample.

by

Optional column name(s) in sample defining domains. When given, the result is one row per domain. See "Domains". A column named like one of the table's own, such as n or se, is refused.

variance

How to compute it. "auto" uses the design's own estimator (see "Variance") and falls back to the jackknife when that declines; "analytic" insists on the design's own estimator, returning NA with the reason in note rather than falling back; "jackknife" uses the jackknife, and returns NA with the reason in note for systematic and Poisson samples, where it does not apply; "none" skips it. The result reports which was used in method, and "none" when nothing could produce a figure.

level

Confidence level for the interval.

df

Degrees of freedom for the interval. NULL uses the design's (see "Confidence intervals"); Inf gives a normal interval; otherwise a single number of 1 or more.

alternative

"two.sided" for a confidence interval, "less" for a one-sided upper bound or "greater" for a lower bound, each at level. See "Confidence intervals".

Value

A list of class drawn_ratio with a print() method, holding ratio, the estimate; variable and x, the names of y and x when they are column names, else NULL; total_y and total_x, their estimated totals; and variance, se, ci, level, alternative, df, n, n_random, ci_scale, design, deff, method, note and unreachable as for ht_total(). With by, a drawn_by table with a row per domain and a ratio column, as for ht_total(). Both have coef(), vcov(), confint(), as.data.frame() and tidy() methods; see "Working with the result" in ht_total().

Variance

The ratio is linearised. Its variance is that of the Horvitz-Thompson total of the residuals (y - R x) / X_hat, with X_hat = sum(x / pi) (Särndal, Swensson and Wretman 1992; Deville 1999), and is computed with the design's own estimator, as for a total: see "Variance" and "Confidence intervals" in ht_total() for the estimators, the fallback to the jackknife, the degrees of freedom and the notes. For the designs as_svydesign() hands to survey with identical standard errors, the standard error equals that of survey::svyratio() on its result. For systematic, spread and systematic PPS samples it comes from the estimator this package uses for their totals, which survey does not have.

The residuals sum to zero over the sample, weighted by 1 / pi, so a ratio whose sampled rows lie in one primary sampling unit, one row or one cluster, gets no standard error, as a Hajek mean does. When y is proportional to x in every sampled row the residuals are 0, the variance is set to exactly 0 rather than left to rounding error, and note says so.

The ratio of two estimated totals is biased, by an amount of order 1 / n, which is small against its standard error except in small samples. The design effect compares its variance with that of the same ratio from a simple random sample of the same size, as survey::svyratio(deff = TRUE) does.

Domains

by gives a ratio for each domain, R_d = Y_d / X_d over the rows of the domain, estimated from the whole sample. Each domain's residuals, (y - R_d x) / X_hat_d, are 0 outside it, as for the domain totals and means described under "Domains" in ht_total(), and the standard errors are those of survey::svyby(~y, ~d, design, survey::svyratio, denominator = ~x). A domain whose estimated total of x is 0 is refused by name.

A missing y or x is refused. survey::svyratio(na.rm = TRUE) on as_svydesign() estimates the ratio over the rows that have both.

References

Deville, J.-C. (1999). Variance estimation for complex statistics and estimators: linearization and residual techniques. Survey Methodology, 25, 193–203.

Särndal, C.-E., Swensson, B. and Wretman, J. (1992). Model Assisted Survey Sampling. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4612-4378-6

See also

ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign()

Examples

set.seed(1)
pop <- data.frame(
  id = 1:300,
  site = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), each = 100),
  book = round(stats::rlnorm(300, 6, 1))
)
pop$audited <- round(pop$book * stats::runif(300, 0.9, 1.05))
s <- draw(pop, design_stratified("site", n = 45), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)

# Audited value per unit of book value
ht_ratio(s, "audited", "book")
#> Ratio of Horvitz-Thompson totals  (stratified design, n = 45)
#>   ratio    `audited` / `book`
#>   totals   173,026.7 / 177,573.3
#>   estimate 0.9743956
#>   se       0.007899163  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  0.9584544 to 0.9903367  (t, 42 df)
#>   deff     1.01  (about the same as simple random sampling)
sum(pop$audited) / sum(pop$book)   # the truth
#> [1] 0.9718688

# For each site, from the whole sample
ht_ratio(s, "audited", "book", by = "site")
#> Ratio `audited` / `book` by domain  (stratified design, 95% CI, t, 42 df)
#>  site  n  ratio      se ci_lower ci_upper   method
#>     a 15 0.9874 0.01226   0.9627   1.0122 analytic
#>     b 15 0.9707 0.01336   0.9438   0.9977 analytic
#>     c 15 0.9629 0.01515   0.9323   0.9935 analytic

# The ratio estimator of the total uses the frame's total of `book`, and
# is far more precise than the Horvitz-Thompson total here
ht_total(s, "audited", ratio = "book")
#> Ratio estimate of the total  (stratified design, n = 45)
#>   ratio    0.9743956, `audited` / `book` in the sample
#>   x total  198,996, `book` over the frame
#>   estimate 193,900.8
#>   se       1,571.902  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  190,728.6 to 197,073  (t, 42 df)
#>   deff     1.01  (about the same as simple random sampling)
ht_total(s, "audited")
#> Horvitz-Thompson total  (stratified design, n = 45)
#>   estimate 173,026.7
#>   se       20,306.49  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  132,046.5 to 214,006.8  (t, 42 df)
#>   deff     1.03  (about the same as simple random sampling)
sum(pop$audited)
#> [1] 193398
